newsitem.title: UK: UK price data bodes well for retail inflation.
newsitem.headline: UK price data bodes well for retail inflation.

text.p: The British government's re-election campaign received welcome news on Monday from unexpected falls in raw material and factory gate prices, boding well for retail price figures later this week.

The Office for National Statistics said factory gate prices fell 0.1 percent in the month of March for a year-on-year rise of just 1.0 percent, compared with a rise of 1.2 percent in the year to February.

The data also showed firms paid less for their raw materials in the month. Manufacturers' input prices fell by a seasonally adjusted 0.5 percent. Raw materials now cost on average 7.7 percent less than a year ago.
The ruling Conservatives, well behind in opinion polls ahead of the British election on May 1, said the figures were proof that their policies had delivered a sound economic recovery.
"They show Conservative policies have made Britain a low inflation economy," said Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.
"We are achieving sustainable growth without either inflation or balance of payments problems, building prosperity that lasts."
Private sector economists, who had forecast a small rise in both raw material and factory gate prices, said the figures augured well for low prices in the shops in future.

"These are excellent numbers. They confirm the pound's strength is keeping cost pressures under heavy downward pressure and there is plenty of good news in the inflation pipeline which is yet to feed though to the high street," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
During a lengthy rally spanning seven months, the pound has appreciated by around 17 percent on a trade-weighted basis, helping reduce the cost of key imported raw materials.

March retail inflation figures are due on Thursday. They are expected to show underlying inflation, which strips out mortgage interest payments, edged down to 2.8 percent in the year to March from 2.9 in February, analysts said.

But this would still be some way above the government's and the opposition Labour Party's 2.5 percent target and most economists predict that recent good news on inflation will not be enough to prevent an interest rate rise after the election.

"While today's numbers are very good and suggest inflation is not a real problem for the manufacturing sector, it is just giving us a snapshot on a relatively small part of the economy," said David Coleman, chief economist of CIBC.
The service sector, which makes up a much greater part of the economy has already showed signs of inflationary pressures.

February's inflation data showed that while prices of goods rose by 2.3 percent in the past year, prices of services rose by 3.3 percent. And average earnings data for January showed wage pressures clearly building in the service sector.

"Inflation is much higher in the service sector than the manufacturing sector. So despite today's very good figures, interest rates will probably still have to go up after the election -- our guess is still for a half point rise," Coleman said.
March unemployment figures on Wednesday may also give the government a boost. They are expected to show another large monthly fall, this time of 45,000.

And public sector borrowing requirement figures on the same day are seen showing government borrowing undershot the Treasury's forecast by almost three billion pounds ($4.9 billion) over the 1996/97 financial year.
"This week's figures will be very good from the government's point of view and show inflationary pressures are subdued, unemployment falling and public finances improving," said Loynes.
